It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth, and to reflect that these elaborately constructed forms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner, have all been produced by laws acting around us. These laws, taken in the largest sense, being Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance which is almost implied by reproduction; Variability from the indirect and direct action of the external conditions of life, and from use and disuse; a Ratio of Increase so high as to lead to a Struggle for Life, and as a consequence to Natural Selection, entailing Divergence of Character and the Extinction of less-improved forms. Thus, from the war of nature, from famine and death, the most exalted object which we are capable of conceiving, namely, the production of the higher animals, directly follows. There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
</passage>

response.text: It's worth taking a moment to picture a tangled hillside, thick with plants of every kind, birds singing from the shrubs, insects darting here and there, and worms burrowing through the moist soil—and then to consider that these intricately built forms, so unlike one another and yet so tightly bound together in their dependence, all came about through laws still operating around us today. In their broadest sense, these laws are: growth and reproduction; inheritance, which reproduction almost guarantees; variability, arising both directly and indirectly from environmental conditions and from the use or disuse of body parts; a rate of increase so great that it leads to a struggle for survival, which in turn brings about natural selection, and with it the branching apart of species and the dying-out of forms less well adapted. And so, out of nature's conflict, out of hunger and death, comes the most magnificent outcome imaginable—the emergence of the higher forms of life. There is something grand in this way of seeing life, with all its various capacities, as having been breathed originally into one form or a handful of forms; and in the thought that, even as this planet has kept turning through the ages under gravity's unchanging pull, life has grown from such a humble start into an endless procession of forms—each one beautiful, each one remarkable—that continue even now to take shape.
